```{r, include = FALSE}
# Figures are drawn on the real CPB canvas (half page is 7.5 cm, full
# page is 15.5 cm) and only displayed smaller. Code is hidden by default
# so that readers who do not use R see the figure and its parameters.
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7.5 / 2.54,
  fig.height = 7.5 / 2.54,
  dpi = 300,
  out.width = "100%",
  dev = if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) "ragg_png" else "png",
  dev.args = list(background = "#eef8ff")
)
```

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(conflicted)
library(ggcpb)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

# Shows the parameters that build a figure, as a small table.
ptab <- function(...) {
  p <- list(...)
  # a backslash n is shown as written, as one types it in params.csv
  value <- gsub("\\n", "&#92;n", unlist(p), fixed = TRUE)
  knitr::kable(data.frame(parameter = names(p), value = value,
                          row.names = NULL),
               align = "l", format = "html", col.names = NULL,
               escape = FALSE, table.attr = 'class="ptab"')
}

# One standard sentence under every figure. `section` is the number of the
# example code at the end, which the sentence links to (`id` is its anchor).
repro <- function(fun, dataset, section, id) {
  cat("<span class=\"repro-title\">**How to reproduce this figure:**</span> ",
      "copy `params.csv`, `generate_plot.bat` ",
      "and the folder `data` with `", dataset, ".csv` to a personal folder. ",
      "Fill in the parameters above in `params.csv` and start the script. ",
      "In R you can call `", fun, "()` instead. Follow the example code in ",
      "[section ", section, "](#", id, ") to create the plot in R. ",
      "Alternatively, the csv file can be read with `read.csv()` and used ",
      "as input to `", fun, "()`.\n", sep = "")
}
```

This vignette extends the [introduction](introduction.html). It shows more
options for the figure types, such as colours, columns, boxplots and maps.
The parameters next to a figure work in Excel, as explained in the
introduction and in the [import vignette](import.html). The same figures can
be made in R. The last sections show what is possible in R only.

# Column charts

The introduction shows columns with a second axis and horizontal bars. This
section shows the position of the columns and the limits of the value axis.

## Stacked columns

With `position = stack` the columns are placed on top of each other. Dodged
is the default position. The legend follows the order of the series. Set
`reverse_legend` to `TRUE` if you want to reverse the legend order.

```{r data-col-stacked}
sectoren <- c("industrie", "diensten", "landbouw", "overheid")
tw <- tibble(
  jaar   = rep(2023:2027, each = 4),
  sector = factor(rep(sectoren, 5), levels = sectoren),
  waarde = c(18.2, 11.5, 24.1, 7.6, 17.4, 12.9, 22.8, 8.1, 19.6, 13.4, 21.5,
             8.8, 20.1, 12.2, 23.3, 9.4, 21.3, 14.0, 22.1, 10.2)
)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r col-stacked}
cpb_col(tw, x = jaar, y = waarde, fill = sector,
        position = "stack",
        title = "Toegevoegde waarde per sector", ylab = "mld euro")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-col-stacked}
ptab(plot_type = "col", title = "Toegevoegde waarde per sector",
     x = "jaar", y = "waarde", fill = "sector",
     position = "stack", ylab = "mld euro")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_col", "col-stacked", "6.6", "code-col-stacked")
```

## Dodged columns

Dodged is the default position, so the columns stand next to each other. The
legend then follows the order of the series.

```{r data-col-dodged}
regios <- c("Noord", "Oost", "Zuid", "West")
scenarios <- c("basispad", "beleidsvariant")
scenario <- tibble(
  regio    = factor(rep(regios, each = 2), levels = regios),
  scenario = factor(rep(scenarios, 4), levels = scenarios),
  effect   = c(2.4, 3.1, -0.8, 1.2, 4.6, 5.2, 1.9, 3.3)
)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r col-dodged}
cpb_col(scenario, x = regio, y = effect, fill = scenario,
        title = "Effect per regio en scenario", ylab = "% mutatie")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-col-dodged}
ptab(plot_type = "col", title = "Effect per regio en scenario",
     x = "regio", y = "effect", fill = "scenario", ylab = "% mutatie")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_col", "col-dodged", "6.7", "code-col-dodged")
```

## Limits and percentages

The value axis follows the data. It starts and ends where the data does. Use
`value_limits` to set the limits yourself, such as 0 and 100 for a share.
`pct_axis` writes the values as percentages. The axis widens when the data
runs past the limits. With `value_crop` set to `TRUE` the data outside the
limits is cut off, with a warning.

```{r data-col-limits}
groepen <- c("boven 3x modaal", "2 tot 3x modaal", "1,5 tot 2x modaal",
             "1 tot 1,5x modaal", "120% wml tot modaal", "tot 120% wml")
auto <- tibble(
  inkomensgroep = factor(groepen, levels = groepen),
  share         = c(13, 14, 19, 26, 35, 62)
)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r col-limits}
cpb_col(auto, x = inkomensgroep, y = share,
        orientation = "horizontal", pct_axis = TRUE,
        value_limits = c(0, 100), width = 0.6,
        title = "Huishoudens zonder auto", ylab = "inkomensgroep",
        xlab = "aandeel huishoudens")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-col-limits}
ptab(plot_type = "col", title = "Huishoudens zonder auto",
     x = "inkomensgroep", y = "share", orientation = "horizontal",
     pct_axis = "TRUE", value_limits = "0;100", width = 0.6,
     ylab = "inkomensgroep", xlab = "aandeel huishoudens")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_col", "col-limits", "6.8", "code-col-limits")
```

# Boxplot styles

The introduction shows the default style of `cpb_box()` and the extended
boxplot. `box_style` sets how a box is drawn. This section shows the other
styles. All styles need the quantiles in columns, so aggregate the data
first.

## James style

`james` is the box of the old James plotter. It has no border, and a black
median that sticks out. The value of the median is printed above it.

```{r data-box-james}
groepen <- c("boven 3x modaal", "2 tot 3x modaal", "1,5 tot 2x modaal",
             "1 tot 1,5x modaal", "120% wml tot modaal", "tot 120% wml")
kk <- tibble(
  groep = factor(groepen, levels = groepen),
  p5  = c(0.23, -1.23, -2.29, -3.35, -4.98, -6.19),
  p25 = c(2.30, 0.60, -0.21, -1.47, -2.83, -4.38),
  p50 = c(3.48, 2.01, 0.91, 0.16, -1.62, -3.06),
  p75 = c(4.92, 3.30, 2.39, 1.37, -0.27, -1.75),
  p95 = c(6.77, 5.39, 4.04, 3.37, 1.54, -0.11)
)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r box-james}
cpb_box(kk, x = groep,
        p5 = p5, p25 = p25, p50 = p50, p75 = p75, p95 = p95,
        box_style = "james", orientation = "horizontal",
        title = "Koopkracht per inkomensgroep", subtitle = "inkomensgroep",
        ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-box-james}
ptab(plot_type = "box", title = "Koopkracht per inkomensgroep",
     x = "groep", p5 = "p5", p25 = "p25", p50 = "p50", p75 = "p75",
     p95 = "p95", box_style = "james", orientation = "horizontal",
     subtitle = "inkomensgroep", ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_box", "box-james", "6.9", "code-box-james")
```

## Modern style

`modern` has light blue boxes, a thick dark blue median and the values of the
quartiles below the box. The values are printed by default. Use `box_labels`
to turn them off and `label_accuracy` for the rounding. `james` and `modern`
draw boxes of one colour, which is set by `fill_colour`.

::: {.figrow}

```{r box-modern}
cpb_box(kk, x = groep,
        p5 = p5, p25 = p25, p50 = p50, p75 = p75, p95 = p95,
        box_style = "modern", orientation = "horizontal", width = 0.35,
        value_accuracy = 0.1,
        title = "Koopkracht per inkomensgroep", subtitle = "inkomensgroep",
        ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-box-modern}
ptab(plot_type = "box", title = "Koopkracht per inkomensgroep",
     x = "groep", p5 = "p5", p25 = "p25", p50 = "p50", p75 = "p75",
     p95 = "p95", box_style = "modern", orientation = "horizontal",
     width = 0.35, value_accuracy = 0.1, subtitle = "inkomensgroep",
     ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_box", "box-modern", "6.10", "code-box-modern")
```

## Grouped boxes

`group` places the categories under bold group names. All boxes share one
value axis. A group with one category of the same name, such as Totaal,
takes one row. `colour_index` takes one palette position per group, so
the boxes of a group share a colour. `value_axis = top` puts the value axis along the top of the figure. This
works for horizontal boxes. A grouped figure is taller, so this one is saved
with `height = 11.4`.

```{r data-box-grouped}
inkomen <- c("tot 120% wml", "120% wml tot modaal", "1 tot 1,5x modaal",
             "1,5 tot 2x modaal", "2 tot 3x modaal", "boven 3x modaal")
bron <- c("Werkenden", "Uitkeringsgerechtigden", "Gepensioneerden")
categorieen <- c("Totaal", inkomen, bron)
ink <- tibble(
  cat = factor(categorieen, levels = categorieen),
  grp = factor(rep(c("Totaal", "Inkomensgroepen", "Inkomensbron"),
                   c(1, 6, 3)),
               levels = c("Totaal", "Inkomensgroepen", "Inkomensbron")),
  p50 = c(0.09, 0.02, 0.07, 0.07, 0.06, 0.04, 0.05, 0.09, 0.04, 0.05)
) |>
  mutate(p25 = p50 - 0.08, p75 = p50 + 0.07,
         p5 = p25 - 0.35, p95 = p75 + 0.35)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r box-grouped, fig.height = 11.4 / 2.54}
cpb_box(ink, x = cat, p5 = p5, p25 = p25, p50 = p50, p75 = p75, p95 = p95,
        group = grp, box_style = "james", orientation = "horizontal",
        value_axis = "top",
        colour_index = c(7, 5, 2),
        width = 0.45, title = "Inkomenseffecten plannen stelsel",
        ylab = "verandering in 2025 (%)")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-box-grouped}
ptab(plot_type = "box", title = "Inkomenseffecten plannen stelsel",
     x = "cat", p5 = "p5", p25 = "p25", p50 = "p50", p75 = "p75",
     p95 = "p95", group = "grp", box_style = "james",
     orientation = "horizontal", value_axis = "top",
     colour_index = "7;5;2",
     width = 0.45, ylab = "verandering in 2025 (%)", height = 11.4)
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_box", "box-grouped", "6.11", "code-box-grouped")
```


## Grouped boxes in the extended style

The extended boxplot of the introduction takes `group` too. The categories
stand under bold group names, as in the grouped boxes above. The figure is
saved on the full page width, so a long list of categories fits. This one has
15 categories and is saved with `height = 16`.

```{r data-box-extended-grouped}
groepen2 <- c("tot 120% wml", "120% wml - mod.", "1 - 1,5x mod.",
              "1,5 - 2x mod.", "2 - 3x mod.", "boven 3x mod.",
              "nog extra boven", "groep 8", "groep 9")
categorieen2 <- c("Totaal", groepen2, "Werkenden", "Uitkeringsgerechtigden",
                  "Gepensioneerden", "Inkomensbron 4", "Inkomensbron 5")
ink2 <- tibble(
  cat = factor(categorieen2, levels = categorieen2),
  grp = factor(rep(c("Totaal", "Inkomensgroepen", "Inkomensbron"),
                   c(1, 9, 5)),
               levels = c("Totaal", "Inkomensgroepen", "Inkomensbron")),
  p50 = c(0.09, 0.02, 0.07, 0.07, 0.06, 0.04, 0.05, 0.04, 0.05, 0.06,
          0.09, 0.04, 0.05, 0.06, 0.07)
) |>
  mutate(p25 = p50 - 0.12 - 0.05 * sin(seq_along(p50) * 1.9),
         p75 = p50 + 0.12 + 0.05 * sin(seq_along(p50) * 2.7 + 1),
         p5  = p25 - 0.15 - 0.06 * sin(seq_along(p50) * 3.1),
         p95 = p75 + 0.15 + 0.06 * sin(seq_along(p50) * 1.3 + 2))
```

```{r box-extended-grouped, fig.width = 15.5 / 2.54, fig.height = 16 / 2.54}
cpb_boxplot_extended(ink2, x = cat, group = grp,
                     p5 = p5, p25 = p25, p50 = p50, p75 = p75, p95 = p95,
                     title = "Koopkracht naar inkomensgroep en -bron",
                     ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

::: {.below}

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-box-extended-grouped}
ptab(plot_type = "boxplot_extended",
     title = "Koopkracht naar inkomensgroep en -bron",
     x = "cat", group = "grp", p5 = "p5", p25 = "p25", p50 = "p50",
     p75 = "p75", p95 = "p95", ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie",
     page = "full", height = 16)
```

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_boxplot_extended", "box-extended-grouped", "6.12",
      "code-box-extended-grouped")
```

# Colours

The colours of a figure follow from the parameters `colour` or `fill`. This
section shows how to choose them.

## Default colours

Map a column to `colour` or `fill` and the series get the house colours. The
order is the same as in the published figures. It is blue, magenta and
taupe, followed by the other colours. A line chart and a column chart of the
same series have the same colours. A single series is blue by default. The section [One colour](#one-colour)
shows how to choose another colour.

```{r data-colour-default}
reeksen <- c("arbeidsproductiviteit", "tfp", "arbeidsvolume")
groei <- tibble(
  reeks = factor(rep(reeksen, each = 10), levels = reeksen),
  jaar  = rep(2015:2024, 3),
  waarde = c(1.2, 0.8, 1.5, 0.3, 0.9, -1.4, 3.1, 1.6, -0.2, 0.7,
             0.9, 0.2, 1.1, -0.4, 0.6, -1.9, 2.8, 1.0, -0.7, 0.3,
             0.4, 1.2, 1.8, 1.1, 0.5, -0.9, 1.6, 2.1, 1.3, 0.8)
)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r colour-default}
cpb_line(groei, x = jaar, y = waarde, colour = reeks,
         title = "Standaardkleuren van reeksen", ylab = "%")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-colour-default}
ptab(plot_type = "line", title = "Standaardkleuren van reeksen",
     x = "jaar", y = "waarde", colour = "reeks", ylab = "%")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_line", "colour-default", "6.1", "code-colour-default")
```

## Colours by position

The house palette has nine colours. Use `colour_index` to choose them by
position. The position of a colour does not change when the default order
changes.

```{r swatches, fig.width = 15.5 / 2.54, fig.height = 1.6}
sw <- cpb_cols()
op <- par(mar = c(2.5, 0, 0.5, 0), bg = cpb_tokens()$bg)
barplot(rep(1, 9), col = sw, border = NA, space = 0.1, axes = FALSE,
        names.arg = seq_along(sw), cex.names = 0.8)
par(op)
```

Choose the positions yourself to keep a series on its colour, for example
after you reorder the levels. Do the same when you rebuild a published
figure.

::: {.figrow}

```{r colour-positions}
cpb_line(groei, x = jaar, y = waarde, colour = reeks,
         colour_index = c(7, 5, 4),
         title = "Gekozen kleuren op positie", ylab = "%")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-colour-positions}
ptab(plot_type = "line", title = "Gekozen kleuren op positie",
     x = "jaar", y = "waarde", colour = "reeks",
     colour_index = "7;5;4", ylab = "%")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_line", "colour-positions", "6.2", "code-colour-positions")
```

## Ordered classes

Ordered classes, such as income groups, need a ramp from light to dark. The
default colours are meant to be distinct, so they do not show an order. Set
`colour_index` to `continuous` for the ramp. The word `discrete` gives the
default colours again. The words `qualitative`, `sequential`, `discr` and
`blues` name a palette.

```{r data-colour-ramp}
klassen <- c("0 tot 5%", "5 tot 10%", "10 tot 20%", "20 tot 30%",
             "meer dan 30%")
intensiteit <- tibble(
  jaar   = rep(2024:2027, each = 5),
  klasse = factor(rep(klassen, 4), levels = klassen),
  n      = c(60, 120, 180, 90, 50, 70, 130, 170, 100, 60,
             80, 125, 160, 110, 75, 90, 120, 150, 120, 95)
)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r colour-ramp}
cpb_col(intensiteit, x = jaar, y = n, fill = klasse,
        position = "stack",
        colour_index = "continuous",
        title = "Geordende klassen", ylab = "aantal personen, x 1000")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-colour-ramp}
ptab(plot_type = "col", title = "Geordende klassen",
     x = "jaar", y = "n", fill = "klasse",
     position = "stack", colour_index = "continuous",
     ylab = "aantal personen, x 1000")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_col", "colour-ramp", "6.3", "code-colour-ramp")
```

## A palette with positions

`colour_index` takes positions or the name of a palette, not both. Use
`palette` to choose a palette and `colour_index` to choose the colours in it.

::: {.figrow}

```{r colour-palette}
cpb_col(intensiteit, x = jaar, y = n, fill = klasse,
        position = "stack",
        palette = "blues", colour_index = c(2, 3, 4, 5, 6),
        title = "Posities in een palet", ylab = "aantal personen, x 1000")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-colour-palette}
ptab(plot_type = "col", title = "Posities in een palet",
     x = "jaar", y = "n", fill = "klasse",
     position = "stack", palette = "blues",
     colour_index = "2;3;4;5;6", ylab = "aantal personen, x 1000")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_col", "colour-palette", "6.4", "code-colour-palette")
```

## One colour

A single series has one colour. `line_colour` sets it for a line and
`fill_colour` for columns. A colour from outside the palette is possible
as a hexadecimal code, such as `#820050`. Be sure to use colours that are 
allowed for the publications. 

```{r data-colour-single}
tfp <- dplyr::filter(groei, reeks == "tfp")
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r colour-single}
cpb_line(tfp, x = jaar, y = waarde, line_colour = cpb_cols(3),
         title = "Een reeks in een gekozen kleur", ylab = "%")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-colour-single}
ptab(plot_type = "line", title = "Een reeks in een gekozen kleur",
     x = "jaar", y = "waarde", line_colour = "#820050", ylab = "%")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_line", "colour-single", "6.5", "code-colour-single")
```

# Maps

The introduction shows a map with classes. This section shows a map with
numbers and a map of provinces. All maps use the boundaries that come with
the package, so no other packages are needed. A map keeps its real
proportions. `save_cpb(preset = "map")` makes it as tall as it needs. The
regions are joined by their CBS code, such as `GM0014`, or by their name.
A region without a value is not filled and a region that is not found gives a
warning.

## Numbers on a map

A numeric `value` gets the sequential gradient and a colour bar. The unit
goes in `subtitle`. A map has no value axis, so `ylab` does not exist.
`reverse` turns the gradient around and `na_fill` fills the regions without
a value.

```{r data-map-numbers}
codes <- unique(cpb_nl_geo("gemeente")$code)
gemeenten_ct <- tibble(
  code  = codes,
  index = round(100 + 12 * sin(seq_along(codes) / 9), 1)
)
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r map-numbers}
cpb_map(gemeenten_ct, region = code, value = index,
        title = "Voorbeeldindex per gemeente",
        subtitle = "index (Nederland = 100)")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-map-numbers}
ptab(plot_type = "map", title = "Voorbeeldindex per gemeente",
     region = "code", value = "index",
     subtitle = "index (Nederland = 100)")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_map", "map-numbers", "6.13", "code-map-numbers")
```

## Provinces

`level = provincie` draws the provinces and `corop` draws the COROP regions.
The default level is `gemeente`. A text value gets the house colours.
`border_colour` sets the colour of the borders. White gives more contrast on
a map with two classes. `legend = bottom` puts the legend below the map and
`none` removes it. A region without a value, here Utrecht, is not filled.
Set `na_fill` to fill it with a colour or a position in the house colours.
An item called "Geen gegevens" is then added to the legend, or "No data" when
`style` is english. A title wider than the map gives a warning of `save_cpb()`.
Break it with `\n`, as is done here.

```{r data-map-provinces}
namen <- unique(cpb_nl_geo("provincie")$name)
provincies <- tibble(
  naam   = namen,
  klasse = factor(rep(c("onder gemiddeld", "boven gemiddeld"), 6),
                  levels = c("onder gemiddeld", "boven gemiddeld"))
) |>
  dplyr::filter(naam != "Utrecht")
```

::: {.figrow}

```{r map-provinces}
cpb_map(provincies, region = naam, value = klasse, level = "provincie",
        colour_index = c(2, 6), border_colour = "white",
        title = "Groei ten opzichte van het\nlandelijk gemiddelde")
```

<div>

#### Relevant parameters {-}

```{r par-map-provinces}
ptab(plot_type = "map",
     title = "Groei ten opzichte van het\\nlandelijk gemiddelde",
     region = "naam", value = "klasse", level = "provincie",
     colour_index = "2;6", border_colour = "white")
```

</div>

:::

```{r, results = "asis"}
repro("cpb_map", "map-provinces", "6.14", "code-map-provinces")
```

# More possibilities in R

The figures in this section need R. Every function returns a ggplot2 object,
so you can add layers and scales with `+`. See also the section on ggplot2
in the [introduction](introduction.html).

## A line over stacked columns

A decomposition has stacked columns and the total as a line. This is
`cpb_col()` plus a `geom_line()`.

```{r overlay, echo = TRUE, out.width = "50%"}
componenten <- c("kapitaal/uren", "arbeidssamenstelling", "tfp")
dec <- expand_grid(
  jaar = 2000:2024,
  # reversed levels stack the first component nearest to zero
  component = factor(componenten, levels = rev(componenten))
) |>
  mutate(bijdrage = round(0.4 + 0.9 * sin(jaar * 1.3 +
                                            as.numeric(component) * 2), 1))
totaal <- dec |>
  summarise(bijdrage = sum(bijdrage), .by = jaar)

cpb_col(dec, x = jaar, y = bijdrage, fill = component,
        position = "stack", colour_index = c(2, 5, 6), width = 0.75,
        title = "Opbouw productiviteitsgroei", ylab = "%") +
  geom_line(
    data = totaal,
    mapping = aes(x = jaar, y = bijdrage, colour = "arbeidsproductiviteit"),
    linewidth = 0.55, inherit.aes = FALSE
  ) +
  scale_colour_cpb_manual(index = 1) +
  labs(colour = NULL) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE, order = 1),
         colour = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
  theme(legend.box = "horizontal", legend.box.just = "top")
```

## Boxes with a fill per year

Map `fill` and pass a `position_dodge()` for two boxes per category. This
works with the default style `ggcpb` only.

```{r box-dodged, echo = TRUE, out.width = "50%"}
kk2 <- expand_grid(kk, jaar = factor(c(2026, 2027))) |>
  mutate(across(p5:p95, \(q) q + (jaar == "2027") * 0.8),
         groep = factor(groep, levels = rev(groepen),
                        labels = c("tot 120%\nwml", "120% wml\ntot modaal",
                                   "1 tot 1,5x\nmodaal", "1,5 tot 2x\nmodaal",
                                   "2 tot 3x\nmodaal", "boven 3x\nmodaal")))

cpb_box(kk2, x = groep,
        p5 = p5, p25 = p25, p50 = p50, p75 = p75, p95 = p95,
        fill = jaar, position = position_dodge(width = 0.6),
        colour_index = c(6, 2),
        title = "Koopkracht per jaar, 2026 en 2027",
        ylab = "% koopkrachtmutatie")
```

## Adding a forecast window manually

The parameter `forecast_x` draws the forecast window for you, as shown in the
introduction. You can also draw it yourself with `annotate()`. A white
rectangle covers the forecast years, a dashed line marks the start and a text
names the window. The new `scale_x_continuous()` replaces the one of the
function, and ggplot2 tells you so in a message.

```{r forecast-manual, echo = TRUE, out.width = "50%"}
bbp <- tibble(jaar  = 2015:2027,
              index = round(100 * 1.02^(jaar - 2015) +
                              1.5 * sin(jaar * 1.7), 1))

cpb_line(bbp, x = jaar, y = index,
         title = "Bruto binnenlands product",
         ylab  = "index (2015 = 100)") +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 2024.5, xmax = Inf, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "white", alpha = 0.4) +
  annotate("text", x = 2026, y = 104, label = "raming",
           size = 2.2, colour = "#666666",
           family = cpb_font_family(), fontface = "italic") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2024.5, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2027, 3), minor_breaks = 2015:2027,
                     guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE))
```

## Export

`save_cpb()` writes a figure at the page width. It is 7.5 cm for `half`,
15.5 cm for `full` and 6.8 cm for `small`. The height is the report height,
unless you set `height`. Use `preset = "map"` for a map and `dpi` for the
resolution. Text sizes are absolute, so the size of the canvas is part of the
design. Draw at the page width and scale only the display.

```{r export, echo = TRUE, eval = FALSE}
p <- cpb_col(auto, x = inkomensgroep, y = share, orientation = "horizontal")
save_cpb("koopkracht.png", p, page = "half")
save_cpb("koopkracht_breed.png", p, page = "full", height = 8 / 2.54)
```

# Example code to create figures in R

The code below creates the figures above in R. It first builds the data,
then draws the figure. It is the same code that made the figures in this
document. Start the script with these lines.

```{r code-library, eval = FALSE, echo = TRUE}
library(conflicted)
library(ggcpb)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

options(ggcpb.style = "dutch") # style of the whole publication
```
